Citation:

R. v. Shearing

Date:

20000204

2000 BCCA 83

Docket:

CA024142

Registry:
Vancouver

COURT OF APPEAL
FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

REGINA

RESPONDENT

AND:

IVON SHEARING

APPELLANT

Before:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Cumming

The Honourable Madam Justice Rowles

The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald

R.C.C. Peck, Q.C., M. Tammen

and N. Harris

Counsel
for the Appellant

W. Smart, Q.C.

Counsel
for the Respondent

Vancouver,
British Columbia

3-4
November 1999

Vancouver,
British Columbia

February 2000

Written Reasons by:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald

Concurred in by:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Cumming

The Honourable Madam Justice Rowles

Reasons for Judgment of the Honourable
Mr. Justice Donald:

NATURE OF APPEAL

[
1
]  Ivon Shearing led the Kabalarian Philosophy for many
years.  It was a tightly knit organization resembling a secular religion and
very much under the influence of its leader.

[
2
]  Mr. Shearing was indicted for sex offences on some
of his followers.  The indictment charged 20 counts relating to eleven
complainants and spanned the years 1965-1990.  On 17 November 1997, a jury
returned verdicts of guilty on twelve counts involving seven complainants and
acquitted him of four counts involving four complainants.  The Crown entered a
stay of proceedings on one count.  The trial judge directed verdicts of
acquittal on three counts and directed conditional stays on the convictions of
three counts of gross indecency on the authority of
R. v. Kienapple

(1974), 1 S.C.R. 729
.  I have appended to these reasons a table setting out the
disposition of the charges.

[
3
]  Mr. Shearing appeals from these convictions.

ISSUES

[
4
]  The issues in the case are set out in the
appellant’s factum as follows:

1. The Learned Trial Judge erred in
failing to sever the counts in the Indictment relating to the complainants,
K.W.-G.. and S.G. (counts 3-9).

2. The Learned Trial Judge erred in
admitting the counts relating to the complainants, K.W.-G.. and S.G. as similar
fact evidence in the proceedings.

3. The Learned trial Judge erred by
limiting the Appellant’s cross examination of the complainant, K.W.-G.

4. The Learned Trial Judge erred in
failing to correctly instruct the jury with respect to the pre-1983 law on
authority and consent.

[
5
]  Mr. Peck, counsel for Mr. Shearing, divided the
complainants into two groups: the sisters K.W.-G. and S.G. in one group and the
remaining complainants in the other.  The basis for the segregation was the
difference in circumstances as between the two groups.  Notably, the G. sisters
lived with their mother at the Kabalarian Centre (“the Centre”) which was
located at 1160 West 10
th
Avenue in Vancouver and which was also the
residence of the appellant.  The other complainants resided in their own
homes.  Further, the alleged offences against the G. sisters began at a younger
age and were of a more serious nature than the offences associated with the
other complainants.

[
6
]  At trial the defence moved to sever the counts relating
to the two groups.  The trial judge refused the motion reasoning that, since
there was sufficient similarity between the counts to admit the evidence of one
against the other as similar fact evidence, all counts should be heard
together.

[
7
]  Mr. Shearing alleges on this appeal that the trial
judge erred in refusing to grant the severance motion and in characterizing the
evidence as similar fact evidence.  Mr. Peck argued the similar fact point
first and at greater length than the severance point because he conceded that
if he could not persuade us that the trial judge was wrong on the similar fact
ruling he had no realistic chance of disturbing the severance ruling.

[
8
]  As I have concluded that the similar fact ruling was
not in error, I will focus my remarks on that aspect of the case and say
nothing more about severance.

[
9
]  This appeal involves two additional grounds.  The
first relates to the scope of cross-examination on a diary kept by K.W.-G..
during an eight month period while she was living at the Centre.  Mr. Shearing
alleges that his counsel was unduly inhibited by the trial judge in exploring
the question why K.W.-G.. made no entry about what Mr. Shearing was doing to
her.

[
10
] The trial judge ruled that in balancing K.W.-G.’s
privacy against the probative value of the disputed line of questioning the
privacy interest should prevail.  He found the probative value of the evidence
sought to be adduced was slight.  For reasons that follow, I do not think that
the trial judge wrongly decided the issue.

[
11
] The final ground of appeal alleges an error in the
charge to the jury.  In his instructions to the jury, the trial judge did not
distinguish between those offences which occurred before the
Criminal
Code
was amended in 1983 and those which arose after the amendment.
The amendment added the exercise of authority to the list of factors which
could vitiate consent in assault cases.  The trial judge told the jury that
they could consider authority as a vitiating element on all the charges where consent
was an issue.

[
12
] On the authority of this court in
R. v.
O’Connor
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14987 (BC CA)
, 14 C.R. (5
th
) 384, this was not a correct
instruction for the pre-amendment counts.

[
13
] The error is said to have infected the other counts
on which guilty verdicts were returned because the trial judge allowed the jury
to use the evidence of each count in relation to every other count.

[
14
] Mr. Smart, counsel for the Crown, conceded the error
but said that it did not affect the outcome.

[
15
] I have concluded that the error may have affected
the outcome but only on the indecent assault counts relating to C.K. and J.V. I
have not been persuaded that the guilty verdict on those counts could have
influenced the jury in reaching verdicts of guilty on the other counts.

[
16
] In the result, I would allow the appeal by setting
aside the conviction and ordering a new trial on the C.K. and J.V. counts; but
in all other respects I would dismiss the appeal.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND

[
17
] A brief description of the Kabalarian Philosophy
will help to put the events in context.

[
18
] The Philosophy was the creature of Alfred Parker,
Mr. Shearing’s predecessor.  It is derived from Eastern religions and takes its
name from the collection of Jewish writings known as the Kaballah.  The goal is
to ascend levels of consciousness toward enlightenment.  The Philosophy teaches
that sexual experience can be a stepping stone to a higher level of
consciousness.  Of particular importance to this case is the means by which a
child’s development can be advanced by the intervention of the leader in
correcting “disembodied minds” in the sexual area.  This is described in the
appellant’s factum at para.9:

It is the duty of parents to teach their children to develop
their minds.  Unbalanced minds continue after the death of a body and can be
dangerous to living minds by becoming disembodied minds.  A living person who
is in a negative state of mind is in danger of drawing from the plane of
disembodied minds.  A person who is having a sexual problem could attract from
the negative sexual plane of mind.  That person would then need a session to
remove the disembodied mind through a medium.  This is referred to as “mental
work” and could be performed by Mr. Parker and later by Mr. Shearing.

[
19
] The Centre at West 10
th
Avenue served as
the hub of the Philosophy’s activities.  It was customary for the leaders to
reside there and for the other members to live nearby.  Mr. Shearing gave
instruction there and a number of complainants said that he performed sexual
acts with them in the den of that house.  The Philosophy also owned a hall
located at 5912 Oak Street in Vancouver and a summer camp on Lake Kalamalka
called the Kalaway Bay Resort.

[
20
] It was in this setting that the allegations of
sexual misconduct by Mr. Shearing arose.  Because the similar fact evidence
issue plays a large part of this appeal I find it necessary to provide a
summary of the evidence of each of the seven complainants in respect of whom a
conviction was recorded.

K.W.-G.

[
21
] K., her younger sister S.G., and
her mother moved into the Centre when K. was seven years old.  She resided
there until she was 20.

[
22
] K. described her childhood as very
hard and restrictive.  She and her sister were expected to do many chores,
abide by the Kabalarian dress code, and refrain from associating with
non-Kabalarian children.  She also described being beaten by her mother.

[
23
] The first incident of Mr. Shearing
touching K. occurred when she was twelve years old.  He told her not to tell
anyone, especially her mother.

[
24
] K. described numerous incidents of
sexual touching in the den, the stairwell and the shower. In one incident in
the den Mr. Shearing spoke of “removing disembodied planes of mind” and told
her he was going to make her into a beautiful young lady.  Acts of intercourse
began when K. was 13. These events occurred approximately once per month and
continued until she moved out of the house.

[
25
] K. testified that she allowed these
acts to occur because she worried that if she complained about them her mother
would be forced to leave the Centre.

[
26
] K.’s association with the
philosophy ended in 1975.  At the time of the trial K. had commenced civil
proceedings against Mr. Shearing and the Kabalarian Society.

S.G.

[
27
] S.G. moved into the Centre when she
was six years old and resided there until she was 18. She described life at the
Centre as a “living hell”.

[
28
] The first incident of sexual
touching occurred when she was twelve.  Mr. Shearing tickled her and touched
her breasts.  After that, whenever she was alone with him he would try to touch
her breasts.

[
29
] When S.G. was 13 Mr. Shearing told
her that he was thinking of making her an “instrument” and she must trust him
completely. He then fondled her breasts and told her not to tell anyone.

[
30
] Between the ages of 13 and 18, S.
performed oral sex on Mr. Shearing at least 30 times.  When she was 14 he
performed oral sex on her and this occurred at least 50 times over the next
four years. They first had intercourse when S. was 18.

[
31
] S.G. testified that Mr. Shearing
never asked her permission with respect to the sexual acts.  She always
regarded them as sexual acts.  She lived in the house and just did what she was
told to do.

C.K.

[
32
] C.’s parents joined the philosophy
when she was nine years old.  C. participated in the Teenage Class, attended
the Kabalarian Correspondence School and went to the Kalaway Bay Resort in the
summers.

[
33
] Mr. Shearing first kissed C. when
she was 13 in September or October 1970.  The next incident of sexual touching
occurred in 1971.  Similar incidents took place approximately four times per
month, usually in the den at the Centre, until C. was about 19.

[
34
] C. testified that during the
touching Mr. Shearing told her that he wanted to remove a condition or plane of
mind that was affecting her. When she was about 16 the discussion turned to her
potential to become a medium.

[
35
] C. described three other incidents
of sexual touching, two taking place at Kalaway Bay Resort (1972 “float plane
incident” and 1973 “Oasis incident”) and the third at the Centre when she was
staying overnight.

[
36
] C. ceased involvement with the
philosophy at about 23 or 24 years of age.

J.V.

[
37
] J.V. became a Kabalarian at age
five when her mother joined the philosophy.

[
38
] In 1972, Mr. Shearing performed a
mental demonstration with R.C. during which he placed one of J.V.’s hands on
his leg. It was revealed by Mr. Shearing that the mind of a dead priest had
been raping J.V. in her sleep.  After Ms. C. had left the room, Mr. Shearing
touched and kissed J.V.’s breasts and told her that she was a beautiful young
woman and that this experience brought her mentally closer to him and the
“principle”.

[
39
] A series of sexual touching
incidents occurred in the den at the Centre.  There was one instance of digital
vaginal penetration.

[
40
] J.V. testified that she did not
regard the touching as being sexual acts, but that Mr. Shearing was trying to
help her mentally.  She would not have allowed it to occur had she believed it
was for his sexual gratification.

[
41
] J.V. remained a spiritual follower
of Mr. Shearing until 1995.

J.T.

[
42
] J.T.’s parents were members of the
philosophy when she was born in 1965.  She attended Kabalarian Correspondence
School and participated in the Teenage Class until she was 21.

[
43
] J.T. described an instance of
sexual touching which occurred in the den at the Centre in 1984 when she was
aged 19. Mr. Shearing performed a mental demonstration with R.C. whereby the
voice of a priest came through Ms. C. and indicated that J.T. had sexual
“hang-ups”. Mr. Shearing admonished the priest and put him to sleep. After Ms.
C. left the room, Mr. Shearing offered to “help” J.T. and rubbed her breasts
and placed his hand into her panties. He then placed her hand on his penis at
which point J.T. said she did not wish matters to go further and he stopped.
J.T. did not believe that the acts had been for Mr. Shearing’s sexual
gratification.

J.A.

[
44
] J.A. became involved in the
philosophy when she was eight years old.

[
45
] There were a number of incidents of
kissing and sexual touching which occurred at Kalaway Bay Resort in the summer
of 1985 when J.A. was 15.

[
46
] Following the summer of 1985, J.A.
met Mr. Shearing in the den at the Centre, usually after she had requested an
interview with him.  During these interviews Mr. Shearing would kiss her and
touch her breasts.  Mr. Shearing told her that he was creating a bond between
them and that it was a link for her to feel close to the principle.  This
occurred approximately 25 times, extending into 1986.  Her contact with Mr.
Shearing ceased when she turned 18.

[
47
] At the time of the events, J.A. did
not think that Mr. Shearing had any sexual motivation, but believed that he was
trying to assist her. She viewed him as a master and a teacher.

[
48
] J.A. became disillusioned when in
August 1995 Mr. Shearing went to the United States.  This made her question his
motivation in touching her.

S.A.

[
49
] S.A. was born in 1969 and her
parents joined the philosophy when she was seven years old.

[
50
] In 1985, after Teenage Class, Mr.
Shearing took her into the den at the Centre and French kissed her on two or
three occasions.  He first touched her intimately when she was 17.  S.A. had
initiated the meeting because she was seeking counselling from him regarding an
instance of childhood sexual abuse. Mr. Shearing cuddled her and massaged her
breasts.

[
51
] When S.A. was 18, she initiated a
meeting because she was considering seeking professional counselling. Mr.
Shearing cuddled and kissed her and placed her hand over his clothed penis. He
told her the reason he was being intimate with her was because she was obsessed
by a sexual plane of mind that needed to be dealt with.

[
52
] At the time of the events S.
believed that Mr. Shearing was trying to assist her. She would not have
permitted him to touch her if she felt it was for his sexual gratification.

DISCUSSION

[
53
] The analysis of the appeal will
merge the grounds relating to severance and similar fact and, as I mentioned,
my focus will be on the latter aspect.  The other two grounds,
cross-examination on the diary and misdirection on authority and consent, will
be discussed in turn.

1.   Similar Fact

[
54
] Mr. Peck argued that the
allegations in the G. counts differed from the non-G. counts in terms of
timing, the nature and frequency of the acts, the context and circumstances and
the nature of consent.  He submitted that a high degree of similarity was
required in order that the evidence in the G. counts may be used as evidence in
the non-G. counts.  This is because the defence on the G. counts was that Mr.
Shearing did not commit the acts, a general denial, and therefore the use of
the evidence of the other counts as similar acts would go to proving the crimes
themselves and not merely some aspect of them.  The defence position on the
non-G. counts generally was that the complainants consented.  Mr. Peck further
argued that the G. counts involved morally repugnant acts of such gravity that
they would poison the minds of the jury in considering the other counts.  His
ultimate submission was that since the prejudicial effect of the evidence was
so great the probative value (in the sense of close similarity or connection
between the two groups) was required to be of the highest order and, in this
case, it fell short of the mark.

[
55
] I see no difficulty in accepting
Mr. Peck’s underlying propositions.  They appear to be supported by authority
and they provoked very little debate in the hearing before us.  His contention
is not that the trial judge set the threshold too low, but that the trial judge
misdirected himself as to the probative value of the G. evidence and failed
adequately to consider its prejudicial effect.  Since the Crown does not
contend that the trial judge set the threshold too high, the issue joined before
us is whether the evidence was sufficient to clear the threshold.

[
56
] In this case there were some marked
dissimilarities between the two groups of counts and these were noted by the
trial judge in his severance ruling.  But he went on to decide that the facts
satisfied the requisite degree of similarity.  I set out two pertinent excerpts
from his ruling:

Thus, it is accurate to say that there are
significant and multiple similarities in the proffered evidence of the [G.s]
and the evidence already led.  At the same time there are some real and
important dissimilarities.

It is equally true that the [G.] evidence
has a significant prejudicial effect.  I am persuaded also that the [G.]
evidence has significant probative value on the issue of intent with respect to
the other complainants.  Most of the other complainants say that the sexual
acts occurred at a time and in a context where the accused portrayed himself as
bereft of sexual motives, and as a person who was working only for the
spiritual betterment of his then partner.  The accused is expected to testify
that this was the case and that he had no sexual intent.  He will say that the
complainant recognized that at the time and freely and voluntarily gave a valid
and genuine consent.  In my view, the [G.] evidence could be very helpful to a
jury, if it is believed, in assessing the credibility of the accused’s
assertions along those lines.

...

In my view, the prejudicial effect of the
[G.’s] evidence is, in this case, outweighed by its probative value.  The
nature of the sexual acts testified to by the [G.s], their frequency, and the
sorts of things said by the accused to the [G.s] will, if believed by the jury,
assist them in assessing the credibility of an assertion by the accused that
the other acts with the other complainants were not sexual in nature but
intended only to serve a spiritual purpose.  That appears to be the fundamental
issue with regard to those complainants.  It is said that they consented
through fraud, the fraud being the misrepresentation to which I have referred.

The evidence of the [G.s] is highly
relevant to that central issue as it tends to rebut a defence of an innocent
non-sexual purpose and a genuine consent by the complainants.

[
57
] The trial judge’s view of the facts
is entitled to deference.  In
R. v. B.(C.R.),

1990 CanLII 142 (SCC)
, [1990] 1 S.C.R.
717, 55 C.C.C. (3d) 1, McLachlin J. said at 24:

... As pointed out in
Morris
, the
weight to be given to evidence is a question for the trier of fact.
Generally,
where the law accords a large degree of discretion to a trial judge, courts of
appeal are reluctant to interfere with the exercise of that discretion in the
absence of demonstrated error of law or jurisdiction
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
58
] And in
R. v.

Arp
,

1998 CanLII 769 (SCC)
, [1998] 3 S.C.R. 339 Cory J. said at 363:

... As well it must be remembered that a high
degree of deference must be given to the decision of a trial judge on this
issue.  See
B.(C.R.)
,
supra
, at pp. 732-33.

[
59
] In his ruling the trial judge made
no mention of the use of the non-G. counts in proving the G. counts.  The
admission of similar fact evidence was justified the other way, that is, the
probative value of the G. counts in proving the non-G. counts on the issue of
consent.  At first glance this analysis would seem to be incomplete.  But it
must be remembered that the similar fact issue arose in the course of deciding
whether there should be a severance.  The defence applied to sever after the
non-G. complainants testified but before the G.s gave their evidence.  It was
sufficient to dispose of that motion to find that their counts could be
inter-related as similar fact evidence in
some
way.  Since the G.’s
evidence was going in regardless in proof of their separate counts it was not
necessary to determine at that point the full extent of how the similar fact
evidence could be used.

[
60
] That determination had to be made
before the trial judge gave his instructions to the jury.  In his charge, he
left the similar act evidence with the jury on the basis that they could use
the evidence for two purposes: (1) to assess the credibility of the
complainants and (2) to determine whether Mr. Shearing had an honest belief
that some of the complainants consented to the sexual acts.  He said this:

I will now tell you the purposes for which
you can use evidence in one count to help you determine whether the Crown has
proved the guilt of the accused on another count beyond a reasonable doubt.
The first purpose for which you can use this evidence is in helping you assess
the credibility or veracity of a complainant.
You may find, based on your
assessment of the evidence, that the conduct described by one complainant
contains substantial and significant similarities between what she told you and
what you have heard from another complainant.  You may decide that these
similarities amount to a pattern of similar behaviour.
Whether or not you
make that finding is entirely up to you.  If you decide that there is a pattern
of similar behaviour you may take it into account in deciding whether a
complainant whose story is part of that pattern of similar behaviour is true.
It is entirely up to you whether you find that a particular complainant is
telling the truth or not.  If you do find beyond a reasonable doubt that a
complainant is telling the truth then you may use her evidence in your
assessment of the credibility of any other complainant provided you are
satisfied that because of the substantial and significant similarities between
their evidence the story of each of the two complainants is part of the pattern
of similar behaviour which you have found to exist.

The second way you can use evidence of
common characteristics or similarities between the counts is in helping you
decide if the Crown has proven that the accused did not have an honest belief
in consent on those counts where it is open to you to consider such a defence.
These counts are Count 1, involving M.S., Count 18 involving A.R., Count 17
involving C.K., Count 12 involving J.V., Count 20, involving S.A., Count 10
involving C.K., Count 9 involving J.A., Count 14 involving B.F. and Count 16
involving J.T.  You may find, based on your assessment of the evidence, that
the circumstances described by these complainants share substantial and
significant similarities which relate to Mr. Shearing’s belief in the consent
of these complainants.  If you reach that conclusion you may use that evidence
in helping you decide whether the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt
that Mr. Shearing did not have an honest belief in the consent of a particular
complainant.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
61
] He twice warned the jury about the
impermissible uses of the evidence.  Before analyzing the evidence, he said:

... I should caution you that you are not to
use the evidence in one count to infer that the accused is a person whose
character of disposition is such that he is likely to have committed the
offences charged in the other counts.  You can use the evidence of a similar
act only in the way in which I will now instruct you.

[
62
] He repeated the warning after
reviewing the evidence and discussing the permissible purposes for the
evidence.  He preceded that additional warning by reminding them that the use
of the evidence was limited:

You should use the similar fact evidence
only for the purpose of deciding whether the Crown has proved a particular
issue in question.

[
63
] The trial judge told the jury that
they must find “substantial and significant similarities” that amount to “a
pattern of similar behaviour” before relating the evidence of one complainant
to another in assessing their credibility.  This meant that for the G. sisters
the jury could look to a pattern in the narratives of the other complainants to
determine whether the G.s were truthful in saying that Mr. Shearing sexually
abused them.  The defence did not object to the similar fact charge at trial
and with one exception did not attack the charge on appeal.  The exception is
the complaint that the trial judge failed to list the dissimilarities along
with the similarities.  I will deal with that later; my present concern is with
the contention that the evidence was not sufficiently similar to pass the
threshold test of admissibility as similar fact evidence.

[
64
] The trial judge gave the jury seven
examples of similarities:

When deciding whether there are similarities or common
characteristics between any two incidents, you should examine all the
evidence.  Here are some examples of the similarities taken from my notes of
the evidence.  M.S., K.W.-G.., S.G., B.F., J.T., C.K., J.V. and J.A. all allege
that Mr. Shearing placed his hand on their vagina or vaginal area.  All
complainants except for C.K. and B.F. testified that Mr. Shearing placed their
hands on his penis.  Except for J.A. each complainant testified to his having
an erect penis on at least one occasion.  C.K., J.V., A.R., C.K., J.A., M.S.,
J.T., S.G., K.W.-G.. and S.A. all gave evidence that one or more incidents with
Mr. Shearing took place in his den at 1160 West 10
th
Avenue in
Vancouver.  S.G., C.K. and B.F. all testified to being told that they had the
potential to be made instruments. … J.T., J.A. and S.A. were all in their mid
to late teens when the alleged intimate activity with Mr. Shearing began.
Finally, the following complainants testified that Mr. Shearing asked or warned
them not to say anything about the activity to others: B.F., C.K., J.V., J.A.,
M.S., J.T., S.G., and K.W.-G..

[
65
] In addition to these illustrations,
Mr. Smart emphasized an overarching common feature, namely, that all the
complainants were members of the philosophy which dominated their young lives.
The Crown’s case was that the complainants were brought within Mr. Shearing’s
influence who then took advantage of their naivete and youth as young persons
raised on his teachings to take sexual pleasure for religious enlightenment and
self improvement.  The central theme of the prosecution was that Mr. Shearing
showed a pattern of sexual predation within a religious group explained or
excused by his own teachings.

[
66
] The G.s did not accept those teachings
but on their evidence they felt required to submit to him because they were
trapped as a result of their mother’s dependency on the philosophy and their
fear that they would be thrown out of their home if they did not submit.  The
source of the domination was different as between the two groups of
complainants but the close connection with the philosophy and the power of the
leader over young members was the same.

[
67
] In my judgment, the evidence was
such that a reasonable jury properly instructed could find in the words of the
trial judge “substantial and significant similarities” constituting a pattern
and it was proper for the trial judge to let the jury use the evidence as
similar facts if they chose to do so.  I say this mindful of the differences
pressed by Mr. Peck in argument.  The remaining question is whether the trial
judge erred in law by failing to sum up those dissimilarities for the jury.

[
68
] It would have been preferable had
the trial judge recited a parallel list of the differences between the two
groups.  An ideal charge would have contained something like the observations
he made in his severance ruling:

Most of those acts [referring to the G.s]
are quite different from, more severe in their legal consequences, and more
morally repugnant, than what has been testified to by the other complainants.

Thus, it is accurate to say that there are
significant and multiple similarities in the proffered evidence of the G.s and
the evidence already led.  At the same time there are some real and important
dissimilarities.

[
69
] I do not think the jury needed a
review of the particular dissimilarities.  Counsel on both sides presented a
thorough review of the evidence, including a discussion of the likenesses and
dissimilarities of the circumstances relating to the various counts.  The
differences stressed by the defence were obvious and unlikely to be ignored by
the jury in their deliberation on the similar fact issues.  The flaw in the
charge was only an imperfection not amounting in my opinion to a reversible
error.

[
70
] I would dismiss the ground of
appeal relating to similar fact evidence.  It follows that the ground
challenging the refusal to sever the counts must also fail.

2.   Cross-Examination on the Diary

[
71
] When K.W.-G.. moved away from the
Centre she left behind a personal diary.  The diary covered an eight month
period just before her 15
th
birthday, a time when she alleged Mr.
Shearing was sexually assaulting her.  The defence, which came into possession
of the diary, wanted to cross-examine her on its contents.  K.W.-G.. engaged
her own counsel to assert and defend a privacy interest in the diary.  The
trial judge heard argument on the competing interests, full answer and defence
on the one hand and privacy on the other.  He rejected an all or nothing
approach – unrestricted questioning versus total privacy – and ruled that some
aspects of the diary could be used in cross-examination but not others.  He
divided the lines of questioning into five categories and weighed the probative
value to the defence against the privacy of the complainant.

[
72
] The principle category in
contention on the appeal relates to the fact that that the diary contained no
record of sexual abuse. At first glance this appears to be a simple line of
inquiry not engaging the contents of the diary. However, as noted by counsel,
wide ranging examination of the whole diary would likely result as counsel
sought to demonstrate the significance, or otherwise, of the absence of
recorded abuse. For example, the defence would point out passages where one
would expect to find a reference to Mr. Shearing’s conduct. In turn, the
prosecution may have been compelled to fully review the contents to show that
such reference was not in keeping with the apparent purpose of the diary.

[
73
] In disposing of this aspect of the
controversy, the trial judge held that the premise for the questioning, namely
that the expectation that if the acts had occurred the witness would have
recorded them, was founded on a discriminatory belief and myth.  As such the
evidence had little or no probative value.  He reasoned as follows:

Finally, Mr. Tammen wishes to conduct what
might be described as a broad ranging cross-examination, using the diary to
demonstrate that it contains no references to sexual assaults by the accused or
sexual activity with the accused.  In essence, he wants to go to the jury and
argue that the witness has made no “complaint”, if I may use that word, to her
private, confidential diary about the sexual assaults that she now testifies
to.

The privacy interest in an examination or
cross-examination of that sort is considerable, because it can be expected to
touch upon a number of the diary entries in order to demonstrate that, on
occasions when an entry might have been made concerning Mr. Shearing, none was
made.  One has to weigh that against the probative value of it and against
criterion number 4 in
O’Connor
, which is whether the matter is premised
upon any discriminatory belief or bias.

It can hardly be denied that, in a great
number of instances of sexual assaults upon children, probably in most such
instances, the complainant does not make any complaint at the time to adults,
friends or those who are close to him or her.  It should come as no surprise,
then, to find that a child would not confide in her diary that an assault of
that sort has occurred.  Ms. Dickson [K.W.-G..’s counsel] argues strongly that
there is no probative value in a lack of complaint in these circumstances, and
that to allow cross-examination and argument on the issue is premised upon a
discriminatory belief or bias
.

I do not make any ruling about how the
defence may argue its case to the jury, but I am satisfied that on this issue,
the privacy interest outweighs the potential probative value.  In my view, the
probative value of demonstrating that Ms. W.-G.. did not write in her dairy a
description of any particular sexual assault by Mr. Shearing is minimal and the
intrusion upon her privacy is considerable.  Mr. Tammen may not conduct that
particular sort of cross-examination with the diary.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
74
] The essence of this ground of
appeal is whether it can be said that the restriction on cross-examination of
K.W.-G.. with respect to her diary impeded Mr. Shearing’s right to full answer
and defence protected under ss.7 and 11(d) of the
Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
.

[
75
] One factor that sets this case
apart is the fact that the defence was already in possession of the diary. A
problem of this nature usually arises in the context of an application by the
defence for production of personal records in the possession of the Crown or a
third party. The process of determining the admissibility of such records also
tends to settle the scope of cross-examination because it is assumed that
questioning will naturally follow the ruling on admissibility. In this case,
however, no production was required and the issue shifted to the permissible
use of the records.

[
76
]  The trial judge, in making this determination, turned to the
common law rules governing production, relying in particular on the Supreme
Court of Canada judgment
in
R.
v
. O’Connor
,
1995 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, [1995] 4
S.C.R. 411. That approach is not challenged on appeal. It is conceded that the
complainant had a continuing privacy interest in her diary and that such an
interest was relevant to determining the scope of cross-examination.

[
77
]  Mr. Tammen, who presented the argument for Mr. Shearing on the
second and third grounds, advanced two points on this ground. The first point
is that the wrong test was used. The trial judge simply balanced the probative
value of the evidence against the complainant’s right of privacy when, on the
authority of
R.
v
. Seaboyer
,
1991 CanLII 76 (SCC)
, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 577, the
proper question is whether the appellant’s right was
substantially
outweighed
by the complainant’s right. The second and related point is that
in applying the test, the trial judge undervalued the probative value of the
evidence and overestimated the potential impact on the complainant’s privacy.

[
78
]  As I have said, counsel at trial sought to question the
complainant, K.W.-G.., on the absence of any reference to abuse in the diary.
This line of questioning, it was argued, is relevant to the theory of the
defence that the K.W.-G.. fabricated the allegations that Mr. Shearing abused her.
Its probative value, moreover, is said to be evident from the fact that the
diary provided a daily account of activities during a time when the complainant
was allegedly subject to constant ongoing abuse. While the overall position of
the appellant is that there should have been no restriction on
cross-examination in respect of the diary, the submissions before this court
focused on the narrower issue surrounding the absence of any mention of abuse.
As that is the only arguable point, I will not address the contention that no
restriction was justified.

[
79
]  The appellant relies primarily on
R.
v.
Seaboyer
,

supra
, and
R.
v.
Osolin
,
1993 CanLII 54 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R.
595. In
Osolin
,
a sexual assault case, the Supreme Court
of Canada ordered a new trial on the basis that the denial of the opportunity
to cross-examine on the medical records of the complainant deprived the accused
of his right to a fair trial. Writing for the majority on this point, Cory J.
at  663-65 emphasized the fundamental importance of cross-examination as an
element of full answer and defence and accorded it constitutional status under

ss. 7
and
11(d)
of the
Charter
. Such constitutional protection warrants,
he notes, a “broad and generous” interpretation:
R.
v.
Potvin
,

1989 CanLII 130 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 525 at 544.

[
80
]  Cory J. went
on to say that the right to cross-examine was not unlimited, particularly in
the context of sexual assault. Referring to several authorities, including
Seaboyer
,

he observed that a careful balancing should take place to ensure:

(a) “…that the complainant’s cross-examination is relevant and
pertinent and not needlessly extended for improper purposes” (at 667); and

(b) that “a
complainant…not be unduly harassed and pilloried to the extent of becoming a
victim of an insensitive judicial system” (at 669).

[
81
] In
Seaboyer
,
the Supreme Court of
Canada struck down the rape-shield provision as it then appeared in the
Criminal
Code
.
In the course of her reasons McLachlin J. at 611
addressed the nature of the balance to be measured:

The Canadian cases cited above all
pertain to evidence tendered by the Crown against the accused.  The question
arises whether the same power to exclude exists with respect to defence
evidence.  Canadian courts, like courts in most common law jurisdictions, have
been extremely cautious in restricting the power of the accused to call
evidence in his or her defence, a reluctance founded in the fundamental tenet
of our judicial system that an innocent person must not be convicted.
It
follows from this that the prejudice must substantially outweigh the value of
the evidence before a judge can exclude evidence relevant to a defence allowed
by law.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
82
] It is argued that the trial judge in the present
case ruled on the range of cross-examination using a simple balance rather than
the more stringent standard in the underlined passage in
Seaboyer
.

[
83
] The Supreme Court of Canada judgment in
O’Connor

dealt with the rule at common law for the production of therapeutic records and
set forth a five-point analysis which the trial judge adapted for the purposes
of his ruling.  Parliament has since enacted provisions in the
Code

dealing with the subject matter.  These provisions were recently reviewed by
the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Mills
,
1999 CanLII 637 (SCC)
, [1999] S.C.J. No. 68
(Q.L.) (S.C.C.).  For reasons which I will discuss later I am of the view that
the
Mills
decision casts a new light on the question of the
complainant’s privacy and supports the impugned ruling.

[
84
] Before turning to a fuller discussion of
Mills

and its effect on the balancing tests, I wish to examine the argument on the
second of the appellant’s points, namely that the trial judge undervalued the
probative worth of the evidence sought to be adduced in cross-examination and
overestimated its prejudicial effect on the complainant.

[
85
] The trial judge assigned “minimal” value to the
proposed line of questioning.  Implicit in this is an acceptance of the
complainant’s contention, made through her counsel at trial, that the
questioning was premised on the discriminatory belief or biased view that a
child would record sexual abuse in a personal diary, if she kept one, and that
if no such notation was made the allegation of abuse was probably false.

[
86
] In my opinion, it is very difficult to generalize
about the behaviour of diarists and I do not think much can be taken from the
studies of complaints and disclosures in the context of sexual abuse in
predicting what any particular adolescent female would include in her diary.
Much would depend on the personality of the individual and the purpose of
keeping the diary.  In any event, it is sufficient for the present matter to
say that I am not persuaded that the trial judge was wrong in his assessment of
the circumstances.  According to the complainant she was a virtual prisoner at
the Kabalarian Centre under the powerful control of Mr. Shearing, her abuser.
The abuse would have caused her much anguish and humiliation.  These two
factors combine to make it highly unlikely that she would record the abuse.
Moreover, we were given copies of the diary, which I have perused.  The style
and content do not suggest that if abuse had occurred the complainant would
have confided it to her diary.

[
87
] Turning to the other side of the balance, the
prejudice to the complainant, again I defer to the trial judge’s assessment of
the circumstances relating to the possible intrusion on her privacy.  As I have
said, the line of questioning was likely to open up the whole of the diary for
scrutiny.  If it had been possible to confine the questions simply to the fact
that the entries made no mention of the abuse, without getting into the diary
itself, the balance may have tipped the other way.

[
88
] As a general proposition, a personal diary attracts
a high degree of privacy.  In
K.L.V. v. D.G.R.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 7569 (BC CA)
, 95
B.C.L.R. (2d) 322 (C.A.), a civil action for sexual assault, a majority of this
court quashed an order to produce the plaintiff’s diaries and journals, holding
that such materials were entitled to a confidentiality privilege.  Hutcheon J.A.
said at 17:

I found interesting and to some extent relevant the views
of the columnist and wordsmith William Safire expressed in the Thursday, 18
August 1994, edition of
The New York Times
“On Keeping Diaries”:

What right does Congress - or the
cops, for that matter - have to pry into anybody’s personal diary?

All of us - muckrakers, solons and
would-be diarists - should take a serious look at the rush to break the seal of
the self-confessional.  Just as our home is our castle, our mind is our citadel
of privacy - and so should be our mind’s most intimate expressions in a
personal diary.

[
89
] Another American view, which I find apposite, is
that expressed by Joyce B. LaVacca in “Protecting the Contents of a Personal
Diary from Unwanted Eyes” (1988) 19 Rutgers Law Journal 389 at 389-90:

The practice of writing one’s most intimate thoughts in a
private journal is universal.  Japanese women were confiding their emotions to
“pillow books”, kept in slipcases away from a husband’s eye, for centuries
before there was anything like a tradition of diary keeping in the west.  And
World War II set the stage for one of the most famous of all diaries, Anne
Frank’s, kept while Anne was hiding from the Nazis in a secret annex in
Amsterdam, Holland.

Diaries serve as private enclaves in our society.
Teenagers buy diaries equipped with lock and key.  The same expectation of
privacy facilitates the keeping of journals as a lay form of psychiatric
therapy.

Diary writing is said to be “the most democratic of all
literary forms” as it is available to everyone, no matter how circumscribed a
person’s life may be by poverty, illness, war or prejudice.  A diary is a place
where political and moral discussion, affirmation and dissent, may be born and
nurtured; and sheltered from unwanted publicity.  A policy to protect the
intimate contents of a personal diary is therefore compelled by a democratic
society that wishes to foster an individual’s development.

[Emphasis added.]

[
90
] These remarks find resonance in the discussion of
privacy in
Mills
.  At para. 89 McLachlin and Iacobucci JJ. for
the majority stated:

The values protected by privacy rights will be most directly at
stake where the confidential information contained in a record concerns aspects
of one’s individual identity or where the maintenance of confidentially is
crucial to a therapeutic, or other trust-like, relationship.

[
91
] What is meant by the phrase “individual identity” is
understood or can be understood by reference to the majority’s citation of
R.
v. Plant
at para. 81:

This Court recognized these fundamental aspects of privacy in
R.
v. Plant
,
1993 CanLII 70 (SCC)
, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 281 where Sopinka, J., for the majority,
stated, at p.293:

In fostering the underlying values of
dignity, integrity and autonomy, it is fitting that
s.8
of the
Charter

should seek to protect a biographical core of personal information which
individuals in a free and democratic society would wish to maintain and control
from dissemination to the state.  This would include
information which tends
to reveal intimate details of the lifestyle and personal choices of the
individual
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
92
] It is in the nature of most personal diaries that
they will, in the words of
Plant,
“… reveal intimate details of
the lifestyle or personal choices of the individual.”  Being forced to reveal
the contents of a diary is akin to having one’s inner discourse intercepted.
For these reasons, I reject the argument that the trial judge overestimated the
prejudice to the complainant.

[
93
] Returning to the allegation that the trial judge applied the
wrong test, I have formed the opinion that
Mills
has shifted the
balance away from the primary emphasis on the rights of the accused. The
decision requires a reconsideration of the position of the complainant, and in
particular the equality rights of the complainant, so as to effectively guard
against procedures which deny complainants equal access to and benefit of the
law.
Mills
dealt with therapeutic records. It held that the
equality guaranteed in
s. 15
of the
Charter
was engaged by the
fact that disclosure of intimate details of therapeutic records would tend to
discourage reporting of assaults. Disclosure of personal diaries could likewise
have a chilling effect.

[
94
] The majority in
Mills
emphasized the need
to concentrate on the context in which the competing rights arise in order to
strike the right balance in each case.  At para. 89 they drew a bright line in
describing what is not available to the accused in pursuing a defence:

From our preceding discussion of the right to make full answer
and defence,
it is clear that the accused will have no right to
the
records in question insofar as they contain
information that is either
irrelevant or would serve to distort the search for truth
, as access to
such information is not included within the ambit of the accused’s right.

[Emphasis added.]

[
95
] In the present case the trial judge refused
cross-examination on the ground that the appellant’s questioning was
discriminatory.  I think that is the sort of thing that might “distort the
search for truth”.

[
96
] The new direction in
Mills
can be seen
in the summary at para. 94 of the majority reasons:

In summary, the following broad considerations apply to the
definition of the rights at stake in this appeal.
The right of the accused
to make full answer and defence is a core principle of fundamental justice, but
it does not automatically entitle the accused to gain access to information
contained in the private records of complainants and witnesses.  Rather, the
scope of the right to make full answer and defence must be determined in light
of privacy and equality rights of complainants and witnesses.
It is clear
that the right to full answer and defence is not engaged where the accused
seeks information that will only serve to distort the truth-seeking purpose of
a trial, and in such a situation, privacy and equality rights are paramount.
On the other hand, where the information contained in a record directly bears
on the right to make full answer and defence, privacy rights must yield to the
need to avoid convicting the innocent. Most cases, however, will not be so
clear, and
in assessing applications for production courts must determine
the weight to be granted to the interests protected by privacy and full answer
and defence in the particular circumstances of each case
.  Full answer and
defence will be more centrally implicated where the information obtained in a
record is part of the case to meet or where its potential probative value is
high.  A complainant’s privacy interest is very high where the confidential
information contained in a record concerns the complainant’s personal identify
or where the confidentiality of

the record is vital to protect a therapeutic relationship.

[Emphasis added.]

[
97
] In my opinion the trial judge’s ruling conforms with
these principles.  I cannot say that the balance he struck is wrong.

3.   Authority and Consent

[
98
] This ground is restricted to the convictions on
counts 3 and 6 (K.W-G.); 7 and 9 (S.G.); 10 (C.K.); and 12 (J.V.).  These
counts preceded the 1983 amendment of the
Criminal Code
which
added “the exercise of authority” as an element capable of vitiating consent.
The provision is now numbered
s.265(3)
and reads as follows:

(3)  For the purposes of this section, no consent is obtained
where the complainant submits or does not resist by reason of

(a)  the
application of force to the complainant or to a person other than the
complainant;

(b)  threats or
fear of the application of force to the complainant or to a person other than
the complainant;

(c)  fraud; or

(d)

the exercise of authority.

[Emphasis added.]

[
99
] As mentioned, the trial judge gave the same
instruction on authority and consent for all counts even though the amendment
occurred after some of the offences.  Since this court’s decision in
Regina
v. O’Connor
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14987 (BC CA)
, 14 C.R. 5
th
384, decided after the trial
in the present case, a distinction must now be drawn between pre-amendment
cases, where authority can only be considered on the question whether consent
was in fact given, and those following the amendment, where the exercise of
authority can render consent invalid.  It follows that the blanket instruction
was an error in law.

[
100
]     In my judgment the error affects only two
counts, count 10 involving C.K. and count 12 for J.V.  I cannot accept the
submission that the error contaminated the other guilty verdicts on the ground
that the trial judge told the jury that they could use the evidence of one
count in considering the others.  The trial judge also told them that they
should do so only in deciding whether the Crown has proved a particular issue.
The issues in C.K. and J.V. were consent and whether the consent was vitiated
by fraud or the exercise of authority.  For the G sisters it was whether or not
the events happened.  Assuming as I must that the jury followed the trial
judge’s instructions, they would not have taken the vitiation of consent on the
part of C.K. and J.V. as proof of the occurrence of the offences related to the
G. sisters.  The particular issues are not logically connected.

[
101
]      Consent was never a real issue with the G.
sisters.  Since no one suggested that they consented I do not think the jury
would have related the instruction regarding authority and consent to them.
Nor do I think that the fact that the consent of C.V. and J.V. may have been
invalidated would increase the likelihood in the jury’s mind that he committed
the offences against the G. sisters.

[
102
]     As far as the other complainants are concerned,
the jury was entitled to entertain Mr. Shearing’s exercise of authority as a
vitiating element.  The fact that they may have found him guilty on the counts
related to C.K. and G.V. on an improper basis, namely pre-amendment vitiation,
does not affect the validity of the other verdicts.

[
103
]     Mr. Smart questioned the correctness of
O’Connor

and asserted that the decision of
R. v. Jobidon
,
1991 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, [1991] 2 S.C.R.
714 should govern.  In
Jobidon
, Gonthier J. decided that the 1983
amendments merely codified an existing common law rule vitiating consent.  The
rule in question was the public policy against consenting to a fight which
results in bodily harm.  Here the argument is that the exercise of authority
was always a vitiating element at common law and the amendment merely brought
it into the
Code
.

[
104
]
Jobidon
was considered in
O’Connor

and distinguished.  The Crown did not seek leave to appeal
O’Connor
.
The Yukon Court of Appeal has since followed
O’Connor
in
R.
v. L.B.
(1998), 106 B.C.C.A. 154.

[
105
]     An important aspect of
O’Connor

is the recognition of policy questions separating the giving of consent and the
invalidation of that consent.  The court said at 399-400:

The question posed by the Crown (when can consent be said
to be genuine?) is really the same as that posed by the defence in this case
(what factors can be said to vitiate consent?).  At the heart of both questions
is a single inquiry - whether the consent that was obtained was not real, not
valid, impaired or defective.

To look to s.135(a) for a definition of consent which goes
beyond the notion of the conscious exercise of will and into the area of the
“genuineness” or "validity” of the consent is to step into uncertain
territory
.  A wife may consent to have sex with her husband because he
threatens to find another partner if she does not.  Her consent is not
“genuine” or free from pressure - she feels compelled to go along with her
husband’s wishes.  The husband’s behaviour is in some senses coercive, but not
criminal.

Christine Boyle recognized this difficulty in her book,
Sexual
Assault,
where she said, in dealing with the 1983
Code

revisions (at pp. 61-2)
:

It seems to be an enormous task to
begin to assess the culpability involved where a man, for example, takes
advantage of his superior social and economic status and the relative docility
and desire to please of a particular woman, or where sexual intercourse occurs
because of fear of, not force, but negative social repercussions.  Many of us
are reluctant to grapple with these moral issues in our everyday lives, and
parliament has, in a sense, side-stepped the issue by continuing (with some
significant additions) the old approach that was used with rape, that of
listing factors which vitiate consent.  It may well be that, because of the
lack of sophistication of the criminal law, and its need to focus on factors
that are relatively clear-cut in a factual sense, this is the better approach.
Thus future reform may concentrate on refining the list rather than radical
change.

Ms. Boyle adds this footnote:

Depending of course on prevailing
notions of what ought to be criminalized.  As P. Atiyah states in
The Rise
and Fall of Freedom of Contract
(1979), at p.436, “the idea, that a man’s
will is ‘overborne’ by certain types of pressure and not by others is, both in
logic indefensible, and in practice impossible of application.  The reality is
that some forms of pressure are in conformity with the … moral ideas of the
community, and others are not.”

We are of the view that the Legislature set out a complete
set, or list, of factors which vitiate consent in s.135(b).  The structure of
the legislation and the philosophical difficulty in defining “genuine” consent
persuade us that this is so,
as well as the simple point that to look
beyond s.135(b) to find a more comprehensive definition of consent would be to
make s.135(b) redundant.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
106
]     This “uncertain territory” contains many
perplexing issues that do not arise in fight situations.  I am disinclined to
reconsider
O’Connor
.

[
107
]     Mr. Smart also argued that if the trial judge
erred in his charge on authority and consent the error would not have affected
the result and the curative proviso in s.686(1)(b)(iii) should be invoked.
Focusing on C.K. and J.V. he said the real issue was fraud, i.e. whether Mr.
Shearing had deceived them that the acts were for their spiritual advancement
rather than his sexual gratification.  That, I accept, was a probable basis for
the verdict on the C.K. and J.V. counts, but the Crown pressed the consent
issue at trial and cannot now establish that fraud was the only route followed
by the jury in arriving at their verdicts.

[
108
]     Moreover, the jury might have considered
authority and fraud together on the basis that the exercise of Mr. Shearing’s
authority made it more likely that the complainants would be deceived.  Because
of the risk of entanglement of the two elements I do not think it can be said
that the fraud was the only basis for the verdicts.

[
109
]     I do not accept that the error could not have
affected the result.  Accordingly, I decline to apply the curative proviso.

DISPOSITION

[
110
]     For the above reasons I would allow the appeal
with respect to C.K. and J.V. and in all other respects I would dismiss the
appeal.

"The Honourable Mr. Justice Donald"
